analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA of its authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it died in committee at the end of the 112th Congress, leaving EPA greenhouse gas rules in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to bar the EPA from issuing any rule, taking any action, or even considering greenhouse gas emissions for climate purposes, and would remove greenhouse gases from the law's definition of an air pollutant. It would also repeal a series of existing EPA rules — including the agency's 2009 finding that greenhouse gases endanger public health — and invalidate the waiver that lets California enforce its own vehicle emissions standards for model year 2017 and later. It carves out limited exceptions, such as the already-final car and truck fuel-economy rules and greenhouse gas reporting requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil fuel producers, coal-fired power plants, and other large emitters, who would avoid the costs of greenhouse gas permitting rules and future emission standards. State-level efforts to adopt stricter rules would lose federal enforceability, so regulated industries would face one less layer of oversight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from promulgating any regulation concerning, taking action relating to, or even considering greenhouse gas emissions to address climate change, and removes greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of an air pollutant for climate purposes.

Repeals and makes legally void a long list of existing EPA actions, including the 2009 endangerment finding, the greenhouse gas reporting rule, and the permitting 'tailoring' rules that allowed large stationary sources to be regulated.

Bars the EPA from granting — and retroactively invalidates — the waiver allowing states to enforce their own greenhouse gas vehicle standards for model year 2017 and later, while leaving states otherwise free to adopt their own greenhouse gas laws.

Preserves narrow exceptions: the existing light-duty vehicle greenhouse gas and fuel economy standards, the proposed heavy-duty truck standards, the renewable fuel program, federal climate research, ozone-layer rules, and carbon dioxide emissions monitoring and reporting.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, through continued greenhouse gas emissions that the EPA could no longer regulate for climate purposes: more air pollution exposure over time, and the loss of a federal backstop that states could previously rely on or supplement. Proponents argued the reverse — that the public pays through higher energy prices from EPA rules, which the bill's title ('Energy Tax Prevention Act') reflects.

drawbacks.text: The bill would repeal the EPA's scientific 'endangerment finding' and void the legal basis for greenhouse gas permitting of large stationary sources, eliminating the main federal tool for limiting carbon pollution from power plants and factories.

It would invalidate the California vehicle-emissions waiver for model year 2017 and later, taking away a stricter state standard that other states could adopt, though it preserves the already-final federal car and truck standards.

Supporters' honest case: EPA greenhouse gas permitting rules impose compliance costs on manufacturers, utilities, and energy producers, which they argued would raise energy prices and cost jobs — the bill was framed as preventing an 'energy tax.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the industries and businesses facing EPA greenhouse-gas permitting and reporting requirements, the bill offered real regulatory relief. For the public, the trade ran the other way: it would have removed the EPA's core authority to limit greenhouse gases, repealed the endangerment finding, and revoked California's ability to set stricter vehicle standards — with no replacement climate policy offered. The modest exemptions for already-final vehicle standards and reporting rules did not change the overall effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe introduced the bill on March 3, 2011, with 44 cosponsors — 43 Republicans and one Democrat, Sen. Joe Manchin.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, its only substantive action.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
Because the bill did not become law, the EPA's greenhouse gas rules — including the endangerment finding and permitting rules the bill targeted — remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people were better off because the bill died: EPA greenhouse gas rules and the endangerment finding stayed in place. Had it passed, fossil fuel producers and large industrial emitters would have been the main beneficiaries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; EPA climate rules survived

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar EPA greenhouse gas regulation and championed it with introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 43 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the party's leader Mitch McConnell, giving it the backing of most of the Senate Republican conference.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; sole Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democrat to do so.

against.name: Chair Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup; the bill's only action was referral to her committee and it never advanced.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never received a vote or a motion to proceed during the 112th Congress.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: His administration defended EPA greenhouse gas rules and opposed legislation stripping EPA climate authority; the White House threatened to veto the House companion bill that passed in April 2011.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 43 of the Senate's 47 Republicans cosponsored, joined by a single Democrat (Sen. Manchin), while the Democratic-led committee and Senate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and gas producers and large industrial emitters
industries.note: The bill would have repealed EPA greenhouse gas rules, the endangerment finding, and permitting requirements for large stationary sources, sparing these industries compliance costs while leaving the public exposed to unregulated carbon emissions. Its interest in this bill ran directly against public climate and air-quality protections.

The bill preserved the already-final light-duty greenhouse gas and fuel economy standards but revoked the California waiver for stricter state vehicle standards in model year 2017 and later. Automakers that had built plans around the single national standard would avoid a stricter California pathway, while losing the certainty of the existing agreement's future rounds.
The bill explicitly preserved the Clean Air Act's renewable fuel program from its general prohibition, leaving the mandate for ethanol and other biofuels intact.
